question: Kestrel Foods has revenue of £500m, COGS of £300m, receivables of £50m, inventory of £40m and payables of £30m. Calculate its cash conversion cycle.
model_answer_md:
Three ratios, then combine them. Receivables are measured against revenue; inventory and payables against COGS, because that is the basis on which they are carried.

$$\text{DSO} = \frac{50}{500} \times 365 = 36.5 \text{ days}$$
$$\text{DIO} = \frac{40}{300} \times 365 = 48.7 \text{ days}$$
$$\text{DPO} = \frac{30}{300} \times 365 = 36.5 \text{ days}$$

$$\text{CCC} = \text{DIO} + \text{DSO} - \text{DPO} = 48.7 + 36.5 - 36.5 = \mathbf{48.7 \text{ days}}$$

So Kestrel waits roughly **49 days** between paying for its ingredients and collecting from its customers. Every day of that gap has to be funded — which is why it has £60m of working capital tied up.
key_points: DSO uses revenue; DIO and DPO use COGS
It is the funding gap between paying suppliers and being paid
Ties back to the £60m of working capital on the balance sheet

follow_ups.question: If Kestrel halved its DSO, how much cash would that free up?
follow_ups.answer_md: Halving DSO from 36.5 to about 18 days would halve receivables from £50m to £25m, releasing roughly **£25m** of cash — a one-off benefit as the balance unwinds, not a recurring gain. The CCC would fall to about 30 days.

follow_ups.question: Why express it in days rather than pounds?
follow_ups.answer_md: Because days are comparable across companies of different sizes and across years as a company grows. £50m of receivables means nothing on its own; 36.5 days tells you immediately how the collection performance compares with a peer or with last year.

weak_answer_note: Uses revenue as the denominator for all three ratios, or gets the sign of DPO wrong and adds it. A weak answer produces the number without saying what the gap has to be funded by.
